body: Recalling the thoughts of Jean Monnet and the main ideas of the Schuman Plan, the long-term target of the Union was to bring European states closer by entwining their economies and industries. It is not without irony that the complexity of the negations around Brexit proves how successful and far-going European integration has come already. When in June 2016, the people of the United Kingdom (UK) were asked in a referendum whether to remain or leave the European Union (EU), the majority (51.9%) – with a very small margin – voted in favor to leave the Union. Followed by complex negotiations and massive political turbulences, the UK formally left the EU in February 2020. However, after four years of Brexit negotiations and uncertainty, a phase of intense trading negotiations started to draw up the future relationship between the EU and UK until the end of the transition phase to find a final compromise for future cooperation and trade relations. Regardless of the outcome, the departure of Britain triggers severe changes and disturbances on both sides of the Channel. It will open a new chapter of cross-channel relations not only with long-lasting political and economic consequences but also for the environment and future environmental policy-making in Europe. Doubtless, the departure of Britain will change the face of the United Kingdom but it will also leave its traces on the European Union, causing distortions in the short but also in the long term.1

Britain´s departure is expected to trigger serious changes to several realms of the Union, such as for the economy, the financial sector, international trade, international relations, but also for environment-related issues (e.g., climate change, renewable energies, circular economy).

In 2015, the EU adopted its first Circular Economy package that should bring the EU economy in line with sustainability. And with the newly proposed EU Green Deal in 2019, the EU set out an ambitious target to achieve a climate-neutral Europe by 2050. And this goal can only be achieved by rapid progress in establishing a circular economy.

Given that the EU has more experience with enlargement than with reduction, Brexit represents a quite unique phenomenon worth studying. While several countries have joined the Union over the yars, only the UK has left it. This paper seeks to provide answers on how Brexit will affect the EU environmental policy-making, in particular, it focuses on the consequences in the field of the circular economy. Therefore, the work analyzes and evaluates the consequences of Brexit in terms of establishing the European circular economy in two realms: economy and politics. The paper seeks to shed light on possible short-term and long-term consequences.

Though not lucidly defined yet, the circular economy concept builds on economic, natural, and social capital and redefines growth by focusing on society-wide benefits.4 The concept of CE seeks to design out waste and pollution, decouple economic activities from material demand and consumption of resources, and keep valuable materials as long as possible in the system.5 Thus, CE aims at a reduction, reuse, recycling and recovery. CE redefines waste as input material for other industries and focuses on promoting the use of secondary raw materials. This not only includes recycling efforts but includes a view on the overall life-cycle of products.

16 The package was followed by the Circular Economy Action Plan and proposals that cover the full lifecycle of products, from design, production, and consumption to waste management and the development of a stronger secondary raw materials market. The initiatives resulted in a series of legislative and non-legislative actions, such as for waste management, plastics, fertilizers, marine litter, critical raw materials and indicators measuring circularity. The EU also set out targets for recycling (65% of municipal and 75% of packaging waste by 2030) and implemented a ban on landfilling of separately collected waste by 2030. According to the EU plans, the competitiveness of key industry sectors including manufacturing, waste management, and recycling will be strengthened by the Circular Economy Package.

In December 2019, the new European Commission proposed its Green Deal with the aim to achieve carbon-neutrality by 2050. 17 However, achieving the net-zero GHG emissions objective by 2050 requires a profound transformation of value chains across the EU economy based on innovative production processes and new business models. To achieve this ambitious goal, industries in all member countries have to make significant contributions. The new Commission President von der Leyen claimed the European Green Deal to be "Europe's man on the moon moment"18, describing climate policy as Europe’s new growth strategy. According to von der Leyen, the former growth model based on fossil fuels and pollution is out of date. The new Green Deal which is based on ten major pillars not only includes climate-neutrality by 2050 but also the establishment of a circular economy (see Figure 1).
As laid out by several studies, the establishment of a circular economy is
a feasible option to reduce emissions

19 A large-scale switch from fossil-based technologies to low-carbon technology, the expansion of renewable energies, and the promotion of energy-efficiency measures are envisioned. Since efforts will result in increased material demands further triggering greenhouse gas emissions, a net-zero emission reduction objective is only achievable with a drastic system change in material and resource management based on circularity.

The New Green Deal for Europe comprises three distinct institutions: The Green Public Works (GPW) (an investment program), the Environmental Union (package of legislation to align policy with scientific consensus), and the Environmental Justice Commission (EJC) an independent body to research, monitor, and advise EU policymakers. The latter is designed as an international body to ensure that the green transition is also a just one. By its broad mandate, the EJC has the power to set new international standards for research and reporting on environmental injustices. However, the EJC takes only an advisory role, providing data on environmental changes for other EU institutions or developing new indicators to evaluate policies. The GPW aims at delivering Europe’s economic transformation through a large investment program by including aspects of environmental justice and focusing on decarbonizing Europe’s economy, reversing biodiversity loss and guaranteeing decent jobs across the continent. The program is financed entirely through green bonds issued by the European Investment Bank. The Environmental Union aims at a broader target – a systemic change by offering a comprehensive regulatory package to realign policies based on scientific consensus. It is aimed to foster Europe´s position as a global green leader.

The new EU circular economy approach based on new waste and recycling laws will not only represent half of the EU´s efforts to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 but also include measures to ensure access to raw material supplies. Access to critical raw materials (CRMs) used in digital and clean technologies was named as a strategic security question in the European Green Deal. Certain CRMs are irreplaceable in solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles, and energy-efficient lighting, essential technologies for the establishment of a circular economy and the promotion of energy transition.

Although a circular economy is perceived as a necessity to ensure the prosperity and wellbeing of human mankind in the future, its establishment is not self-evolving. Change requires strong political commitment and is often based on economic rationale.

The 2018 Global Environmental Performance Index lists solely European countries under the top 15.21 Switzerland ranks first, followed by France, Denmark, Malta, Sweden. The UK is put on the sixth position while Germany is ranked 13th. However, green and clean does not necessarily correlate with a high level of circularity. Burning waste for energy, as widely practiced in some countries, minimizes landfilling but is not improving recycling rates or establishing circular loops within the industry. In a circular economy, products remain as long as possible in the system, they are shared, reused, repaired and/or refurbished. But when they finally reach their end of life, they are dismantled, recycled and the materials are injected back in the economic cycle. However, CE not only focuses on waste management and recycling but taking a look at every stage of a product's life, starting from the mining of raw materials, design, production, consumption to waste management.

Based on the low self-sufficiency for raw materials in the EU, the physical trade balance is obviously asymmetric. By weight, the Union imports about three times more goods from non-EU countries than it exports. Hence, the Union is very dependent and vulnerable to the import of certain raw materials. According to Eurostat, import dependency climbed from 18.6% (2000) to 23.1% in 2018. To address the issue, in 2008 the Commission launched the Raw Material Initiative, a strategy to secure access to raw materials in the EU. In 2018, the Commission published a report highlighting the potential for a more circular usage of critical raw materials in the economy.22

A circular economy aims to maintain the value of products, materials and resources for as long as possible by returning them into the product cycle at the end of life while minimizing the production of waste. However, modern economies are heavily dependent on a steady and secure supply of raw materials and the demand for materials is increasing with economic development. A recent OECD (2019) report projects the demand for raw materials to more than double by 2060.23 The concept of CE stresses environmental and economic benefits gained by a more circular economic system, mainly by lowering the overall material demand and raw material consumption and increasing resource efficiency as well as developing a secondary raw material market.

The domestic material consumption (DMC) measures the annual amount of materials directly used by an economy.24 In 2000, the DMC of the Union was roughly 7,500 million tonnes (see Figure 2). After a decline due to the financial crisis in 2008, the EU-28 climbed to some 6,900 million tonnes in 2017. Across the EU, material consumption patterns vary largely depending on each Member States´ extraction of domestic resources, population density, living standards, economic development, living standards, the size of agriculture, manufacturing and construction industries, but also the size of its imports and exports market. The amount of consumed material per capita in the EU-28 varies largely. While Finland consumed the most material per (34.5), followed by Estonia (30.9) and Ireland (26.2), the UK only consumes 8.9 tonnes. Spain has the lowest consumption rate across the EU-28 with 8.4 tonnes. In 2018, the total DMC of the EU economy stood at about 13.8 tonnes per capita.25 And much of it still ends up as waste. In the EU, the amount of municipal waste generated per person in 2018 amounted to 492 kg (2008: 518 kg), and about 490 kg in 2017.26 Municipal waste production of the UK was with 463 kg below average. In 2004, the UK´s waste production peaked at 602 kg. The top three waste producers are Denmark (766 kg), Malta (640 kg) and Cyprus (637). At the bottom of the list, we find Poland (329 kg) and Romania (272 kg). The recycling rate of municipal waste of the EU-28 (2018) was at 47%. The top recycling countries are Germany (67.3%), Slovenia (58.9%), Austria (57.7%), while the UK shows a rate of 44.1%. Although not the core idea of a circular economy, recycling of materials helps to improve circularity as it can be re-introduced into the economy as new substances or products.

Since 2000, the resource productivity of the EU economy increased by around 40% but has been stagnating for the last three years (see Figure 3).27 Before the financial and economic crisis in 2008, the resource productivity growth was rather modest, it picked up in the following years. Since then, we can observe clear decoupling effects. However, to achieve a further decoupling, more drastic changes are required to curb material consumption while upholding GDP levels. At the country level, we can see that the resource productivity varies largely among the Member States (see Table 1). The highest resource productivity is recorded in the Netherlands (84.4% above the EU-28 average), followed by the United Kingdom (66.3%) and Luxembourg (44.7%). While Germany is close to the EU-28 average, Italy lies 58.1% above the EU-28 average, France about 19.2% above, Spain 38%. On the other hand, Poland reaches only 50.2% of the EU-28 levels. This indicates that the EU has moved towards a more export-oriented economy whilst being more and more involved in globalization.

The UK imports and exports large quantities of products in raw, semi-manufactured and finished forms. It is a net importer of materials, with its material footprint climbing a staggering 43% between 1997 and 2007, followed by a reduction of 20% in the aftermath of the 2008-crisis. Between 2012 and 2016 it increased by 6%.28 By 2016, materials embodied in imported goods make up 78% of the UK´s material footprint.

The circular material use rate in the EU was 11.2% in 2017. 32 In the period between 2004 and 2012, it increased from 8.2% to 11.1%. However, since 2012 the rate has fluctuated between 11.1% and 11.2% with a small increase in 2016 (11.4%). In the period between 2010 and 2017, the circular material use rate increased in 15 of the 27 Member States, remained stable in three and decreased in nine other Member States (see Figure 5). The highest increases were recorded in Italy (+6%), followed by Latvia, Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands (+5%). At the opposite end of the scale, the largest drop was recorded in Luxembourg (-15%) and Finland (-11%), followed by Spain (-3%) (Eurostat, 2020c). The UK´s circular material use rate reached 17.8% in 2017 (2013: 15.7%). It was the third-highest after the Netherlands (29.9%) and France (18.6%).

For the establishment of a circular economy, a large market with fewer restrictions, no border controls, and lower transaction costs is preferred, as economies of scale can be realized. The establishment of a competitive secondary raw material market must be preceded by setting up common quality standards for secondary raw materials. Europe-wide trade of secondary raw materials is essential, but if materials and goods are carried with fossil-based vehicles, the question of sustainability remains unsolved. Trade in recyclable raw materials of EU-28 increased only slowly from 9,183,737 tonnes (2014) to 9,433,896 in 2018. Trade in the UK grew slightly from 118,835 tonnes (2014) to 133,885 tonnes in 2018. On the contrary, in France, it dropped from 711,107 tonnes to 470,383 over the same period.

As laid out above, progress in increasing the circularity rate is slow. However, digitalization may help to overcome some impediments in closing loops. 33 The implementation of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) within the End-of-Life processing of products aims to close the information gap among all involved actors (designer, producer, consumer, and waste management).34

However, widely applied usage of CPS requires the infrastructure, and 5G telecommunication infrastructure is believed to provide this backbone for Industry 4.0 and circular economy.35 While the UK is one of the pioneering countries in 5G deployment, the industrial powerhouse Germany along with other countries struggle to provide digital infrastructure for Industry 4.0 and CE. Digitalization provides new space for platform-based enterprises focusing on circular efforts, engaging in new business models based on renting or leasing.36 At the end of life, manufacturers take back the product including all the precious materials for refurbishing, reselling, or recycling. In this scenario, design for easy dismantling, refurbishing and repair is key. Companies are rethinking their business models and adapt the ownership structure of their products (e.g., pay per washes, pay per lux) and provide leased products.

Implications of Brexit for Political Dynamics in the Union
During the enlargement process, the influence of each individual state on decision-making has declined gradually.
Thus, for gaining leverage over EU decision-making, building

In the EU, groups of member states with more or less close ties form coalitions to influence the decision-making process. Basically, such coalitions emerge at an early stage, often during the informal approach to formal talks in the European Council and the Council of the European Union.
And since proposals can only be rejected by a group, Britain’s departure will have a major impact on relations in the Council of the European as new coalitions need to be formed to advance with CE.
According to the Lisbon Treaty, approval of decisions in the Council requires at least 55% of votes from Member States and 65% from share-of-population votes.

Britain clearly utilized its EU membership to steer European policy-making in its favor.40 While the country supported more than 97% of the legislative measures adopted by the Council between 2004 and 2016, London voted against proposals more often and showed relatively higher abstention scores (see Figure 6) than others. Germany is the second-largest veto player but on different issues than the UK. Closest with the UK on passing proposals come Denmark, Sweden, and the Netherlands.

A Franco-German Coalition for Circular Economy?

As a result of Brexit, the importance of large member states (Germany, France, Italy, Spain, and Poland) increases, as their voting power gains are greater. A blocking minority can be achieved with 13 member states voting against, or at least four member states representing more than 35% of the EU’s population. France and Germany together represent 33.2% of the EU’s population. In a different constellation, France, Italy, and Spain together represent 39.24% of the European population and can therefore easily form a blocking minority (Kleinowski, 2019).

In the past, the Union's political integration was mainly driven by a Franco-German coalition. Paris and Berlin were the primary architects for closer integration in monetary, foreign, security, as well as justice affairs. 43 London often voiced skeptical and critical voices, attempting to steer discussions in its favor.
EU legislation should be efficient and market-oriented

. London has relentlessly criticized the burden of the tight regulatory framework of the EU. Furthermore, British environmental NGOs have played a crucial role in the creation of EU-level ENGOs and influencing European environmental policy-making.44 London was an advocate for a reduction of regulations with the aim to reduce the bureaucratic costs for small and medium-sized enterprises in the internal market. Whereas London often called for more market-based instruments, Germany prefers approaches based on binding regulatory instruments. Brexit silences these critical voices, while others have more space. Poland is the largest Central and Eastern European member, and its solid economic performance provides Warsaw with legitimacy to join discussions. However, in the past Poland showed no strong engagement in promoting strict environmental policies (e.g., renewable energies). In the EU-27, the voice of climate laggards such as Poland, Hungary or the Czech Republic could turn louder. These countries blocked a new EU climate change target and refused to support writing the target into the EU’s strategic program for 2019-24. Sharing a communist past and poor environmental records, the Visegrád group could - led by Warsaw - further slowdown EU efforts in stepping up circular economy efforts.

In another option, we could see a coalition between Germany and the eight northern European member states. Finance ministers of these countries already met in 2018 to start talks about alternative proposals for reforming the Eurozone. On various matters, such as the environment, monetary, fiscal, EU budget, their viewpoints are close to Germany's. However, despite this close relationship with its Northern neighbors, Berlin will not risk its uniquely close bilateral relationship with Paris. Thus, the political realm about CE is still in limbo.

Modernization and promoting sustainability, such as decarbonizing production processes gain relevance but there are discussions on how to promote such a major systematic transition. Are large industrial actors the main drivers or is change driven by the integration of a regional ecosystem of resilient actors, enabling diversity of approaches (open source)? While it is not clear yet which approach prevails over the other, some countries prefer certain approaches. Larger investments in a future-oriented European industry are supported by several Member States (i.e., the Netherlands, Benelux Germany, France, Poland, Spain). However, the four large member states Germany, France, Italy and Spain show little interest in promoting the digitalization of their economies, mainly out of fear of a decline in their traditional manufacturing industries. On the other hand, the Netherlands, the Nordic countries, Ireland and Czechia, see digitalization as an opportunity, also promote a sustainable economy. Among the policy areas where London took great interest during its membership were economic policies, global free trade, foreign affairs, security, defense, internal market consolidation and budgetary matters (e.g., the Multi-annual Financial Framework). The Union’s annual budget lays down all expenditures and revenues and ensures the funding of EU policies and programs. The largest source of EU revenues (67%) stems from member-states transfers based on gross national income (GNI). After Germany and France, the UK was the third largest net contributor to the EU budget
. London contributed roughly €13bn (2018) to the total EU budget (about 9%), and Brexit rips a
large hole in the EU budget

With difficulty, the EU managed to set up its 2020 budget of about €168.7bn (2019: €165.8bn) by rising the contributions from member states.46 The budget covers seven large areas, with the biggest part allocated to Sustainable Growth (€59.9bn), followed by Economic, social and territorial cohesion (€58.6bn), Competitiveness for growth and jobs (€25.3bn), Global Europe, and Administration (each €10.3bn). Large parts (ca. 40%) are spent on agricultural policy and farming. In the past, London heavily criticized the Union´s agricultural policy for its high costs. There is concern that agriculture continues to take up most part of the budget while other areas encounter cuts in their finances. After the massive stimulus programs due to Covid-19 outbreak, the Union needed to readjust its budget. Given that the EU is left with lower financial contributions and due to the massive economic distortions in 2020, environment-related programs could receive lower funding, including circular economy efforts. As of now, the concrete consequences of Covid-19 are not comprehensible and cannot be discussed in detail here. However, the pandemic clearly showed how vulnerable global supply chains are and how important the availability of locally produced goods is. In this respect, the virus outbreak is likely to bring back some production lines to Europe over the mid-term. While it is unrealistic to think that globalization stops completely, there are strong calls for strengthening the local or regional production. From a historical point of view, such external shocks proved to have the power to change the economy drastically. Future shortages of certain goods and raw materials due to the closures of borders in Europe and worldwide can only be avoided by promoting a strong local industry based on closed loops. However, the crisis takes its toll on companies´ investments in innovation and digitalization. As a result, European governments and the EU wrapped up previously unseen financial stimulus programs. However, calls from some EU Member States were loud to abandon the Green Deal in order to have more financial resources to restore the “conventional” economy. 47 Properly designed, such large financial supports could be used as instruments to stimulate green and sustainable circular efforts in the EU. As of now, it is too early to say how the programs will impact EU circular efforts.
